---
title: "Business Critical analysis"
description: "The whole Business Critical route in the order you meet it, from the determination to the obligations that outlast the work."
---

Some analysis carries consequences large enough that it is named, registered and assured
differently. Being Business Critical changes what happens at several points in the lifecycle, and
most of those points are covered in full by another section, which this page links to rather than
restating.

This page is the route, in the order you meet it, for someone who has just been told their work is
Business Critical and needs to know what that means for them this week.

It does not decide whether your work is Business Critical. That is settled at scoping, and it is
settled once. Step 1 says how.

## 1. At scoping: is it Business Critical?

*Covered in full in [section 4, the analytical lifecycle](/guidance/04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd).*

{{< include /guidance/_partials/bca-determination.qmd >}}

## 2. Name who is accountable

*Covered in full in [section 3, roles and responsibilities](/guidance/03-roles-and-responsibilities/index.qmd).*

Business Critical work needs a named Analysis Senior Responsible Officer: senior enough to carry the risks
across the lifecycle, and the person who approves that the work is fit for purpose before it is
used. Settle who that is now, not at sign-off, because the register entry needs the name and
because they should see the work while it can still change.

Section 3 defines the role, who it can be, and how it relates to the commissioner, the analyst and
the assurer.

## 3. Read the assurance level

*Covered in full in [section 5, deciding your assurance level](/guidance/05-deciding-your-assurance-level/index.qmd).*

{{< include /guidance/_partials/bca-assurance-level.qmd >}}

{{< include /guidance/_partials/diagram-assurance-level.qmd >}}

## 4. Get it on the register

Where analysis or a model is Business Critical, **it must be logged with the Data Science, Advanced
Analytics and Statistics team, who add it to the register.**

GovS 010 puts the register as a *should*; for Business Critical work this playbook requires it. What
the standard asks the entry to hold is the list below.[^src-govs-010-section-6-11]

- **a named officer accountable for it**
- **a statement of its intended use**
- **up to date user documentation**
- **guidance on quality assurance**
- **confirmation from the accountable officer that it is suitable for its intended use**

That accountable officer is the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer: a named person senior enough to take
responsibility for the risks across the lifecycle, who approves that the work is fit for purpose
before it is used. This may be the commissioner. The role itself is defined in
[section 3](/guidance/03-roles-and-responsibilities/index.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis, or a model?" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
Both. A model is a particular kind of analytical asset, typically reused over time, and GovS 010
section 6.11 sets specific requirements for models. Analysis that is not a model can still be
Business Critical.

Where the work is a model, the requirements below apply to the model across its whole life, not
just to the run that produced today's number.
:::

## 5. Do the work to the enhanced standard

*The checks themselves are in
[section 6, doing the work](/guidance/06-doing-the-work/index.qmd).*

Business Critical analysis is assured at **Level 4 BCA**, which is everything Level 3 Comprehensive
requires and then more. [Section 6](/guidance/06-doing-the-work/index.qmd) sets out the Level 3
procedure at each phase, and is where the checks themselves live.

What Level 4 adds, in NHSBSA's own words on the decision sheet:

- formal audits
- external review
- additional scrutiny of the documentation
- scrutiny of the structural and conceptual assumptions
- additional scenario testing

With, from this playbook and the Business Critical guidance:

- an analytical assurer from **outside the delivering team**
- code assured against the
  [NHSBSA Analytical Code Assurance Playbook](https://nhsbsa-data-analytics.github.io/nhsbsa-analytical-code-assurance-playbook)
- uncertainty documented and quantified where the method allows, per
  [section 7](/guidance/07-uncertainty/index.qmd), where it is not optional
- a quality assurance statement **published with the output**
- sign-off by the Lead Assurer and then the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer
- a review date set

Where the work is Business Critical, consider explicitly whether those using and assuring it have
the skills and knowledge required, and whether specialist induction or training is needed.[^src-govs-010-section-6-11]

### The documentation stack

The eleven documents below are the full stack, in the order NHSBSA recommends completing them,
with the role that owns each. For an analysis that already exists, start by reviewing what is
there, find the gaps, and fill them before going on.[^src-bca-assurance-journey]

![](/static/diagrams/14-bca-documentation-stack.png){fig-alt="Eleven documents in a numbered column, each with the role that owns it, beside three panels covering the four named owners, the quality assurance appraisal and what happens after sign-off. All of it is set out in the text below the picture."}

<details>
<summary>Text description of this diagram</summary>

**The stack, in the order the guidance recommends completing it**, and who owns each part.

| | Document | What it holds | Owns it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Analytical plan | The question, the purpose, why the decision matters, the commissioner, the dates | Team |
| 2 | Scope | The decisions it supports, inputs and outputs, boundaries and limitations, resources, principal risks | Lead Analyst |
| 3 | Assurance level decision sheet | Whether it meets the requirements of Business Critical analysis. Saved and attached to the Specification | Commissioner and Analyst |
| 4 | Specification | Calculations, assumptions, expected accuracy, and the testing that shows it meets its purpose | Lead Analyst |
| 5 | Quality assurance plan | The register of assurance actions: owner, priority, progress, target date, tied to appraisal reference codes | Lead Analyst |
| 6 | QA appraisal, basic information | Model name, identifier and contact, and the four named owners | Lead Analyst |
| 7 | The analysis or model itself | No template, because models differ. The Model Guidance Document instead. Fills the data, assumptions and risk registers | Lead Analyst |
| 8 | Technical guide | Enough for someone with no prior knowledge to take over its operation and development | Lead Analyst |
| 9 | User guide | Enough for a new team member to run it and produce the expected outputs | Lead Analyst |
| 10 | QA appraisal, assurance review | Six worksheets scored, with a reason for each rating and the actions it raises | Lead Assurer |
| 11 | Quality assurance sign-off | The Assurance Report worksheet: what was reviewed, the statement, the risks, and the approval | Lead Assurer, then the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer |

**The four owners every Business Critical analysis names.** The **Analysis Senior Responsible Officer** signs the approval statement that the model is fit for purpose and approved for use. The
**Lead Assurer** owns the assurance review and the review statement. The **Lead Analyst** owns the
scope, the specification, the model and both guides. The **Commissioner** knows what the analysis
is for and what depends on it. They are recorded on the Named Owners worksheet at step 6.

**One workbook, three stages.** The quality assurance appraisal is twelve worksheets completed at
three points in the life of the analysis rather than in one sitting: basic information at step 6,
as soon as the model has a name; the analysis or model review while the model is built and tested;
and the assurance review at step 10, by the Lead Assurer with the analyst.

**The assurance review scores six areas**: documentation, governance and oversight, structure and
clarity, data and assumptions, verification, and validation. Outputs is a seventh that NHSBSA has
still to define. Every requirement carries a reference code, so a quality assurance plan action can
be traced back to the criterion that raised it: the Scope document is D1. Actions are prioritised
**Must**, essential to address a significant risk, issue or control weakness; **Should**,
recommended to improve quality, robustness or assurance; or **Could**, additional benefit but not
needed for an acceptable level.

**Sign-off is not the end of it.** Quality assurance continues after an analysis is judged fit for
purpose: that it is used as intended with its caveats, that errors are logged, that improvements
are recorded, and that data and assumptions are kept current through scheduled reviews. Any
material change triggers a review of the documentation and of the assurance requirements,
proportionate to the change, and the scope, specification, both guides, the appraisal and the
quality assurance plan are all in scope of that review.

**Where the stack lives, and what it is called.** All analytical documentation is held centrally by
the Quality and Assurance Team, which is the authoritative source and maintains the NHSBSA register
of analytical models. Analysts may keep working copies locally, but each new production version of
the model goes to the team as it is released. Name every file type first and analysis second, so
the stack can be recognised at a glance: Scope_Specification_AnalysisName, User_Guide_AnalysisName.

Quality assurance is rarely linear. A review that raises a question about the method sends you back
to the technical guide, the specification or the scope, and that is the process working rather than
failing.

</details>

## 6. Say what is uncertain

*Covered in full in [section 7, uncertainty, assumptions and limitations](/guidance/07-uncertainty/index.qmd).*

At every other assurance level, quantifying uncertainty is proportionate to the work. Here it is
not optional: uncertainty is documented, and quantified wherever the method allows it. An
assumption that would change the answer if it were wrong is surfaced rather than carried silently.

Section 7 carries the method, the vocabulary for direct and indirect uncertainty, and what to write.

## 7. Publish what was checked

*The statement itself is in
[section 9, communicating analysis](/guidance/09-communicating-analysis/index.qmd).*

Business Critical analysis is, by definition, analysis that matters to people outside the team that
made it. Two obligations follow.

**The quality assurance statement is published with the output**, not held internally.
[Section 9](/guidance/09-communicating-analysis/index.qmd) shows what one looks like.

**Where an algorithmic tool informs the decision, an Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard
entry is required.** See [section 10](/guidance/10-ethics-and-transparency/index.qmd).

## 8. Keep it true after first use

This is where Business Critical work most often goes wrong. The assurance is done properly once,
and then the world moves.

**Set a review date.** Anything on the register has one.
[Section 11](/guidance/11-review-and-continuous-improvement/index.qmd) carries the cadence.

**Re-assess when the use changes.** If a model is used for a purpose other than the one it was
designed for, or the context of its use has changed, **the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer approves that
new use before it goes ahead**. GovS 010 section 6.11 puts this as a should; for Business Critical
work this playbook treats it as a condition of staying on the register.

**Re-score the assurance level when the work is reused.** A one-off that becomes a monthly
production run is a different piece of work. See
[section 5](/guidance/05-deciding-your-assurance-level/index.qmd).

::: {.callout-important title="The commonest failure" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
A piece of analysis built quickly for one question turns out to be useful, and is rerun for months
by someone other than its author. Nobody re-assesses anything, because no single moment felt like a
decision. Assumptions valid at one point in time are carried silently forward.

Reuse is a trigger. Treat it as one.
:::

## 9. Review, and revalidate the designation

*Covered in full in [section 11, review and continuous improvement](/guidance/11-review-and-continuous-improvement/index.qmd).*

A designation is not permanent, in either direction. Work that was Business Critical can stop being
so, and work that was not can become so as its use widens. Section 11 carries the review cadence
keyed to the assurance level, and the lessons loop that feeds what you learned into the scoping of
the next piece of work.

Revalidating the designation is part of that review, not a separate exercise.

## What you will need

*Covered in full in [section 12, tools, templates and downloads](/guidance/12-tools-and-templates/index.qmd).*

The register return, the quality assurance statement template and the appraisal workbook all live
in section 12, so that a reader finds them by going to one place rather than by remembering which
section mentioned them.

The route above is the order you meet these in. This is the same seven points as a lookup, for
when you know what you are after and want to go straight to the section that covers it.

|---|---|
| **The determination.** The six impact dimensions that decide whether your work is Business Critical | [Section 4](/guidance/04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd), engagement and scoping |
| **Who is accountable.** The Analysis Senior Responsible Officer, and the approver | [Section 3](/guidance/03-roles-and-responsibilities/index.qmd), roles and responsibilities |
| **What assurance level follows**, and the Very High backstop | [Section 5](/guidance/05-deciding-your-assurance-level/index.qmd) |
| **The checks themselves**, phase by phase | [Section 6](/guidance/06-doing-the-work/index.qmd), doing the work |
| **What must be said about uncertainty**, which is not optional here | [Section 7](/guidance/07-uncertainty/index.qmd) |
| **Revalidation**, and when a designation is reviewed | [Section 11](/guidance/11-review-and-continuous-improvement/index.qmd), review |
